title: Execution Memory
definition: Execution memory is the addressable or named state exposed by a selected machine model for instructions to read and modify.
purpose: Let learners trace data changes without equating runtime memory with disks, files, caches, or every physical memory layer.
history: Machine models have long exposed registers and addressable memory while implementations add caches, virtual memory, and storage systems beneath or beside that abstraction.
mental_model: A numbered table of cells changes over time under explicit read and write rules.
analogy: A labeled workbench resembles temporary working state; it fails because real memory has addressing, representation, protection, and lifetime rules.
common_mistakes: Assuming the teaching table is a physical RAM diagram
industry_notes: System layers expose different memory abstractions; engineers state which layer and lifetime they mean.
ai_notes: AI explanations must label whether they discuss language variables, virtual memory, architecture-visible memory, or hardware.
interview_notes: Ask the candidate to separate temporary execution state from stored files.
exercise_candidates: Classify values as source text, execution memory, output, or persistent storage
lab_candidates: Trace load/store-style operations in a bounded memory table
project_candidates: Define memory bounds and error behavior for the instruction simulator
